title: WHAT IF THE MOON CAME 2X CLOSER?

segments.line: The Moon just moved twice as close.
Watch what the ocean does first.
A silver wall of water races up the
sand right past your ankles,
because the Moon's pull grows about eight times
stronger when it gets twice as close.
You scramble backward up the beach grabbing
your flip- flops as foamy surf climbs
toward the dunes.
Overhead, a giant Moon fills the
sky at about one hundred ninety-
two thousand, two hundred kilometres
instead of three hundred eighty- four thousand,
four hundred kilometres.
What if the Moon came twice as close?
(Title Card: WHAT IF THE MOON CAME 2X CLOSER?)
First, look at the real Moon tonight.
NASA measures its average distance at three
hundred eighty- four thousand, four hundred
kilometres, or two hundred thirty-
eight thousand, eight hundred fifty-
five miles.
It has a radius of one thousand, seven
hundred forty kilometres and orbits Earth
in twenty- seven days along a slightly
oval path.
At perigee, its closest point,
it reaches about three hundred sixty-
three thousand, three hundred kilometres,
or two hundred twenty- six thousand
miles. At apogee,
its farthest point, it swings to about four
hundred five thousand, five hundred
kilometres, or two hundred fifty-
one thousand miles, while drifting about
one inch farther away each year.
Now cut that average distance in half.
(Chapter 2 Card: HALF THE DISTANCE)
Half of three hundred eighty- four thousand,
four hundred kilometres puts the Moon at about
one hundred ninety- two thousand,
two hundred kilometres.
Step outside and look up:
at half the distance, the Moon looks about twice
as wide and covers about four times the
area in the sky.
Normally, you can stretch your arm out and cover
the Moon with your thumb.
Tonight, the glowing cratered rim spills right
past your hand at arm's length.
Through your bedroom window, instead of a small
coin in the corner of the glass, a colossal
silver lantern fills the frame.
Wait: isn't that just a supermoon?
(Chapter 3 Card: SUPERMOON REALITY CHECK)
Time for a supermoon reality check.
According to NASA, a real supermoon
at perigee looks up to fourteen percent
bigger and thirty percent brighter than the
faintest full Moon at apogee.
Fourteen percent is subtle:
you squint at the sky, shrug,
and wonder if your eyes are playing tricks.
Our Moon at about one hundred ninety-
two thousand, two hundred kilometres
would be one hundred percent wider,
twice the width and about four times the
area. Put them side
by side and today's supermoon looks like
a teacup saucer while our giant Moon
looms behind you like a stadium roof until
you tip off your stool.
Now watch what happens after sunset.
(Chapter 4 Card: SILVER NIGHTS)
With a lunar disc covering about four times
the area, clear nights turn into a bright
silver twilight.
You sit on a park bench outdoors reading a
paperback book with no flashlight at all,
while sharp shadows stretch across the path.
Along the street, automatic streetlight
timers get confused by the bright sky
and switch themselves off.
Up in the trees, birds stay awake
chirping at the silver glow,
and a wide- eyed neighbourhood cat paces
the fence wondering where night went.
You turn another page in the quiet park,
thinking a brighter night feels peaceful.
Then the ocean answers.
(Chapter 5 Card: THE OCEAN AWAKENS)
NASA notes that even a real supermoon can
cause higher tides than usual.
Because tidal force follows an inverse-
cube law, halving the Moon's distance
to about one hundred ninety- two thousand,
two hundred kilometres makes its pull on the
oceans about eight times stronger.
Down on the beach, a wave washes under
your beach towel. You drag the
towel higher up the sand, and the
next wave chases your heels again.
You move your towel again and again until
you are clinging to the top of the lifeguard
stand, while harbour boats buck
on their ropes and the tide line marches up the
stone stairs.
Wait until high tide peaks hours later.
(Chapter 6 Card: HOURS LATER: THE COAST)
Hours later, that eightfold tidal pull
turns low coastal streets into shallow
canals. Seawater brims
over the promenade wall and swirls around
lampposts and park benches.
You paddle a yellow rubber dinghy past a
flooded street corner while cheerful crabs take
over a seaside café table.
Then, when low tide arrives,
the ocean pulls back just as dramatically,
leaving harbour boats sitting high and dry
on wide muddy flats far from the pier
stairs. Tired of rowing
past street signs, you paddle home,
climb upstairs, and try to get some sleep.
(Chapter 7 Card: TRYING TO SLEEP)
Inside your bedroom, sleeping under a
Moon twice as close is a losing
battle. Silver moonlight
pours through the gap in your curtains like a
searchlight aimed straight at your bed.
You pull the curtains tight, slip on a
thick sleep mask, and even stack
sunglasses over the mask, yet the whole
room still glows silver.
Your cat perches on the windowsill batting
at moonbeams while you hide under heavy
pillows and grumble at the ceiling.
Finally you shuffle to the window,
peel back the curtain, and notice how fast
the giant Moon seems to cross the glass.
(Chapter 8 Card: ORBIT AND ECLIPSES)
In our illustration, even if the Moon
keeps its twenty- seven day pace across
the sky, its twice- as-
wide disc makes its cratered edge appear to
race past rooftops and clouds.
And when that giant Moon passes in front
of the Sun during a solar eclipse,
the view is unforgettable.
Today, the Moon barely covers the
Sun. At about one hundred
ninety- two thousand, two hundred
kilometres, a Moon twice as wide
covers far more than the Sun,
turning midday into a deep twilight
around a huge dark silhouette while you watch through
eclipse glasses.
So could the real Moon ever creep closer like this?
(Chapter 9 Card: THE REAL VERDICT)
In reality, NASA measurements show the Moon
is doing the exact opposite.
Instead of moving closer, our Moon at three
hundred eighty- four thousand, four hundred
kilometres is drifting about one inch farther
from Earth every year.
Astronomers track that slow retreat by
bouncing laser pulses off reflectors left
on the Moon. Earth's spinning
tidal bulge tugs our one thousand,
seven hundred forty kilometre radius neighbour
into a slightly wider orbit year after
year. Out on the sand,
you hold up a tiny ruler and wave goodbye
in slow motion. Yet this very
month, the real sky puts on a show.
(Chapter 10 Card: NOVEMBER 2026 SKYWATCHING)
Up on your rooftop at dusk, NASA's
November twenty twenty- six skywatching
tips give you three real nights to mark
down. Before sunrise on
the fifteenth and sixteenth of November,
Mars and Jupiter shine just one point two
degrees apart.
On the seventeenth and eighteenth of November after
moonset, the Leonid meteors
peak with up to about fifteen meteors per
hour. And on the twenty- fourth of
November twenty twenty- six at fourteen
fifty- four U T C,
the first of three supermoons in a row rises,
followed by another on the twenty- fourth of December
twenty twenty- six and a third in
January. Look east around
sunset on the twenty- fourth.
Which night would you watch the giant Moon?
(End Card: IFMOSPHERE · Comment your answer · Subscribe for more what-ifs)
